raw:
{
  "need": "Identity",
  "secondary": { "name": "Competence", "note": "They will be quietly asking 'Can I actually do this job?' before they even sit down at the desk." },
  "read": "A first real job is an identity moment — they are figuring out who they are as a working adult, whether they belong in this professional world, and whether they will be treated as someone capable or just managed. If expectations land as a list of rules, they hear 'we don't trust you yet,' which threatens that emerging professional self before they have had a single day to prove anything.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "Lay out all the rules, consequences, and standards in a thorough orientation speech — feels thorough and fair, but it signals surveillance over collaboration and puts them on the back foot before they have made a single mistake." },
  "mentorMove": "Open the relationship by naming the opportunity and your genuine belief in their capability first, then co-create the working norms together so the standards feel like a shared framework they helped build, not a cage they were handed.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "The core performance and conduct standards are not up for vote — quality of work, showing up reliably, communicating when something goes sideways, treating colleagues with respect.",
    "You will hold the same bar for them as for every other person on the team, because that is what respect actually looks like."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "How they organize their workflow, when they ask questions, which channels they use to communicate, how they prefer to receive feedback — all of that is theirs to shape.",
    "Let them tell you what they need to do their best work in the first few weeks rather than assuming you already know."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 3, "label": "Collaboration" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, welcome to the team — genuinely glad you're here. Before we get into any logistics, I want you to know that I think starting a new job is one of the harder things a person does, and I don't take it for granted that you showed up ready to do this." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "Can I ask — what's one thing you're hoping this role lets you get really good at? And is there anything about the first few weeks that feels uncertain to you right now? I'd rather hear it now than have you figure it out alone." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here's what I'd like to do. I'll tell you the things that are non-negotiable on this team — not because I don't trust you, but because they're what makes the whole team work — and then I want to hear from you how you work best, so we can actually set you up to succeed instead of just hoping it works out." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I'm going to hold you to a high standard here, the same one I hold everyone else to, because I think you can meet it. I'm not doing you any favors if I soften that. What I can promise you is that I will tell you when you're doing well, I will tell you straight when something needs to change, and I will always give you a real shot before I assume the worst. That's the deal I'm offering — does that work for you?" }
  ],
  "longGame": "The relationship you build in week one sets the ceiling for everything else — how candid they will be when they struggle, how much discretionary effort they bring, and whether they see you as someone worth learning from. Invest fifteen minutes of real curiosity now and you buy months of honest, productive work in return."
}
situation: A new hire starts Monday and I want to set clear expectations.
